newsitem.title: USA: NYS Assembly wants state to eliminate sales tax.
newsitem.headline: NYS Assembly wants state to eliminate sales tax.

text.p: The New York State Assembly Speaker, citing a heady rise in retail sales spurred by a one-week moratorium on sales taxes, on Tuesday said he again would try to get Albany to permanently eliminate the tax.

While economists have said that the one-week experiment was unlikely to produce enough data to draw firm conclusions about whether a tax break would alter how much shoppers spend, Sheldon Silver (D-Manhattan) said the program's first few days already had proved its worth.

"For far too long, New Yorkers have fled to other states and taken their shopping dollars with them," Silver said, in prepared remarks. "This sales tax experiment proves that if you reduce the tax burden, shoppers will come."

New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Connecticut all either have lower sales taxes or exempt these items. The one-week tax break for New York State residents, which began January 18, was expected to cost the city up to seven million in revenues and the state as much as $20 million.

The Assembly, which is led by Democrats, in March 1995 approved legislation to end the four percent tax on clothing and footwear that costs less than $500, and give localities the option of dropping all or part of the tax they impose.

New York City Mayor Ruloph Giuliani, a Republican, who testifed before the Joint Legislative Fiscal Committees in Albany, said that he and the City Council Speaker, Peter Vallone, a Democrat, backed phasing out the tax.

Were the city to cut its four percent sales tax by 50 percent, a step Albany would have to approve, he estimated New York City and New York State each would lose $70 million in revenues, assuming the break began on December 1. The state's fiscal year ends on March 31.

However, from $30 million to $40 million of this sum would be made up from other sales and income taxes that would be collected, as the tax break would cause stores to hire more workers, Giuliani told lawmakers, saying the tax break would act like an employment program.

So that while the city and state would lose about $240 million in the first year of a cut, Giuliani predicted they could make up about one-half of that amount, and then over time recover all of the shortfall.

"I can't say that we would over a three- to four-year period make up every dollar of that. I think we would make up 50 percent, 60 percent, maybe we could get as high as 70 percent," he told lawmakers.
As an example, the mayor cited his Administration's decision to cut the hotel occupancy tax, which proprietors said was hurting their business.

While New York City at first thought it would take three to four years to make up the difference, Giuliani said it now was getting $20 million more than when the tax was cut about two-and-a-half years ago.

The yearly cost of eliminating all of the state sales tax has been estimated at around $700 million. In New York City, the total amount of sales tax charged is 8.25 percent, as it includes 0.25 percent for the Metropolitan Transportation Authority.
